_Requirement: Provide text alternatives for any non-text content that is used to convey information such as images, icons, charts, photographs, and animations. The text should provide equivalent information as the visual element. If non-text content does not communicate information, is purely for decoration, used only for visual formatting, or is not presented to users, then it must be implemented in a way that it will be ignored by assistive technology.

exceptions.description: If non-text content is a control or accepts user input, then it has a an accessible name that describes its purpose

If non-text content is pure decoration, redundant to other text content, used only for visual formatting, or is not intended to be presented to users, implement so it will be ignored by assistive technology

_DetectionPatterns: Images without text alternatives (no alt attribute, no aria-label, etc.)
Alternative text containing only white space or generic alternative text such as 'image' or the file name of the referenced graphic
Text alternatives that are redundant to text content of the page
Decorative images not properly marked
Complex images without detailed descriptions

PrimaryFixes.Principle: Add descriptive text alternative that conveys the same information as the image
Examples: Chart ? 'Sales increased 40% from Jan to Mar'

PrimaryFixes.Principle: Mark as decorative so assistive technology ignores it
Examples: Visual separators which are not interactive
User avatar image that precedes a username
Graphic element that is a descendent of a link or button that get their accessible name from an aria-label

PrimaryFixes.Principle: Provide brief alternative plus detailed description
Examples: Chart with data table containing the same information

ValidationCriteria: Alternative text conveys equivalent information
Decorative images are properly marked
Complex content has concise alternative text along with a detailed description in another format (e.g., as tabular data or a long text summary)

Good: Logo: Use company or product name as the text alternative
Functional image: Describe the purpose or action/function of the control the image represents
Informative image: Describe key information conveyed
Animation: Summarize key points of the animation or a high level narrative the animation conveys
Bad: Using generic text like 'image', 'graphic', 'screenshot' (without further context), 'logo', 'photo' or the file name of the graphic
Repeating nearby text exactly
Describing appearance instead of meaning

_Applicability: This rule applies to pre-recorded audio-only or video-only content, except when the audio or video is a?[media alternative for text](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/#dfn-media-alternative-for-text)?and is clearly labeled as such.
_Requirement:
For all pre-recorded audio-only and video-only content created by, for, or licensed to Microsoft: 

- For audio-only presentations and content: caption or provide a text transcript.

- For video-only presentations and content: provide a text transcript, or an audio track. 

The alternative format should present equivalent information as the pre-recorded audio-only and video-only content.
_Guidance: MAS 1.2.1 - Audio-only and Video-only (Pre-recorded) is based on these standards: - WCAG: 1.2.1: Audio-only and Video-only (Pre-recorded) - Section 508: E207.2 WCAG Conformance, E205.4 Accessibility Standard and E205.4.1 Word Substitution when Applying WCAG to Non-Web Documents, and E207.2.1 Word Substitution when Applying WCAG to Non-Web Software. - EN 301 549: PDF of EN 301 549, which applies WCAG principles for Audio-only and Video-only (Pre-recorded) to 9.1.2.1 web, 10.1.2.1 non-web documents, and 11.1.2.1.1 software.

_Applicability:
This rule applies to pre-recorded audio in synchronized media content whether created by, for, or licensed to Microsoft. [Synchronized media](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/#dfn-synchronized-media) content is audio or video synchronized with another format for presenting information and/or with time-based interactive elements unless the media is a [media alternative for text](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/#dfn-media-alternative-for-text)?and is clearly labeled as such.

This rule does not apply to:
- Video players � See MAS 7.1, 7.1.4, 7.3, and 7.6 for rules applicable to video players.
- Video creation and editing tools � See MAS 5.x for rules applicable to authoring tools.
_Requirement: Provide captions for all [prerecorded?audio](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/#dfn-audio)?content in?[synchronized media](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/#dfn-synchronized-media), whether created by, for, or licensed to Microsoft.
_Guidance: MAS 1.2.2 - Captions (Pre-recorded) is based on these standards: - WCAG: 1.2.2 Captions (Pre-recorded) - Section 508: E207.2 WCAG Conformance, E205.4 Accessibility Standard and E205.4.1 Word Substitution when Applying WCAG to Non-Web Documents, and E207.2.1 Word Substitution when Applying WCAG to Non-Web Software. - EN 301 549: PDF of EN 301 549, which applies WCAG principles to Captions (Pre-recorded) to 9.1.2.2 web, 10.1.2.2 non-web documents, and 11.1.2.2 software.

_Applicability: This rule applies to live audio in synchronized media.
_Requirement: Provide captions for all synchronized media containing live (real time) audio (e.g., live product announcements or teleconferences) that is owned by or licensed to Microsoft. Live captions should be synchronized and not obscure on-screen visuals.
_Guidance: MAS 1.2.4 - Captions (Live) is based on these standards: - WCAG: 1.2.4 Captions (Live) - Section 508: E207.2 WCAG Conformance, E205.4 Accessibility Standard and E205.4.1 Word Substitution when Applying WCAG to Non-Web Documents, and E207.2.1 Word Substitution when Applying WCAG to Non-Web Software. - EN 301 549: PDF of EN 301 549, which applies WCAG principles to Captions (Pre-recorded) to 9.1.2.2 web, 10.1.2.2 non-web documents, and 11.1.2.2 software.

_Applicability:
This rule applies to pre-recorded video in [synchronized media](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/#dfn-synchronized-media) created by, for, or licensed to Microsoft. Synchronized media is audio or video synchronized with another format for presenting information and/or with time-based interactive elements unless the media is a [media alternative for text](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/#dfn-media-alternative-for-text)?and is clearly labeled as such. 

This rule does not apply to:
�	Videos for which the significant aspects of the visual content can be understood from the main soundtrack alone. For example, a video of a company representative reading a press release, with no additional visual information shown such as photos or charts, does not require audio description.
�	Video players � See MAS 7.2, 7.3, 7.6, and 7.7 for rules applicable to video players.
�	Video creation and editing tools � See MAS 5.x for rules applicable to authoring tools.
_Requirement:
Provide audio descriptions for all pre-recorded video content created by, for, or licensed to Microsoft, when appropriate (see Note below).

Audio description is additional audible narrative, inserted in natural pauses in the dialogue, which describes the significant aspects of the visual content of visual media that cannot be understood from the main soundtrack alone. It provides information about actions, characters, scene changes, on-screen text, and other visual content.

Note: Audio description is not needed if the significant aspects of the visual content can be understood from the main soundtrack alone. For example, a video of a company representative reading a press release, with no additional visual information shown such as photos or charts, does not require audio description.
_Guidance: MAS 1.2.5 - Audio Description (Pre-recorded) is based on these standards: - WCAG: 1.2.5 Audio Description (Prerecorded) - Section 508: E207.2 WCAG Conformance, E205.4 Accessibility Standard and E205.4.1 Word Substitution when Applying WCAG to Non-Web Documents, and E207.2.1 Word Substitution when Applying WCAG to Non-Web Software. - EN 301 549: PDF of EN 301 549, which applies WCAG principles for Audio-only and Video-only (Pre-recorded) to 9.1.2.5 web, 10.1.2.5 non-web documents, and 11.1.2.5 software.

_Requirement: Information, structure, and relationships conveyed through presentation can be programmatically determined or are available in text.
_DetectionPatterns: Text styled to visually appear as a heading but are not using heading elements or ARIA heading role attributes
Lists formatted visually but not using list markup
Tables lacking necessary column headers, row headers or both
Related content, such as form labels or descriptions, which are not programmatically associated
Custom ARIA markup patterns that contain invalid child elements

PrimaryFixes.Principle: Use appropriate semantic HTML elements to convey content structure. Use ARIA alternatives only when necessary
Examples: nav, main, header, footer, search, aside for important landmark elements

PrimaryFixes.Principle: Programmatically associate related content using ARIA attributes or HTML structures
Examples: aria-describedby for associating related visible information
aria-details for identifying related rich descriptive content that is not an immediate sibling to the element it details
fieldset/legend for groupings of related form controls
caption for providing tables accessible names

PrimaryFixes.Principle: Replace visual-only formatting with semantic markup
Examples: Convert text styled to appear as headings into actual headings
Update heading tags that were used for styling purposes to a more appropriate tag
Use list markup instead of line breaks and unicode bullets
Add table headers for data tables

ValidationCriteria: Content structure is programmatically determinable
Relationships between elements are clear
Information doesn't rely solely on visual presentation

Good: Proper heading hierarchy (h1, h2, h3)
Lists using ul, ol, and li elements
Data tables with th elements for row and column headers
Label element using for attribute to reference ID of the form control it labels
Bad: Fake headings using bold/large text
Lists created with line breaks instead of list elements
Tables without header cells
Form labels that are not associated with the control they are meant to label
Tooltips not being referenced with aria-describedby
Invalid nesting of content (button as direct child of UL element, link as direct child of element with role=row)

_Requirement: When the sequence in which content is presented affects its meaning, a correct reading sequence can be programmatically determined.
_DetectionPatterns: Content order in DOM doesn't match visual presentation, resulting in the content order not being logical when read sequentially
CSS positioning that disrupts logical reading order
CSS flexbox or grid layouts that visually reorder content in a way that disrupts the logical reading order
Tabular data presented out of sequence, because it is not marked up as a table or grid
Multi-column layouts where the columns are meant to be read in a specific order, but the source order is not logical when linearized

PrimaryFixes.Principle: Arrange content in DOM/source order that matches the intended reading sequence
Examples: Match visual layout with markup order
Use CSS for visual positioning while maintaining logical source order
Ensure heading hierarchy follows document structure

PrimaryFixes.Principle: Use CSS positioning techniques that don't disrupt the logical reading order
Examples: CSS Grid and Flexbox with proper order
Avoid absolute positioning that breaks sequence
Test with CSS disabled to verify reading order

PrimaryFixes.Principle: Ensure complex layouts maintain meaningful sequence when linearized
Examples: Tangential content (e.g., sidebars) is placed after main content in source order

ValidationCriteria: Content can be read in a logical sequence
Source order matches intended reading flow
Information maintains meaning when CSS is disabled

Good: Source order matches visual layout left-to-right, top-to-bottom
Main content before sidebar in source order
Logical heading hierarchy (h1, h2, h3)
Bad: CSS grid or flexbox ordering that disrupts reading order
Using CSS absolute position to layout content in a way that doesn't match source order
Content using white space and visual markers such as '|' to create faux tables, but the content is not marked up as a table

_Applicability: This rule applies to websites, electronic documents, and any software that has a user interface.
_Requirement: Instructions provided for understanding and operating content do not rely solely on sensory characteristics of components such as shape, color, size, visual location, orientation, or sound.
_Guidance: MAS 1.3.3 - Sensory Characteristics is based on these standards: - WCAG: 1.3.3 Sensory Characteristics - Section 508: E207.2 WCAG Conformance, E205.4 Accessibility Standard and E205.4.1 Word Substitution when Applying WCAG to Non-Web Documents, and E207.2.1 Word Substitution when Applying WCAG to Non-Web Software. - EN 301 549: PDF of EN 301 549, which applies WCAG principles for Sensory Characteristics to 9.1.3.3 web, 10.1.3.3 non-web documents, and 11.1.3.3 software.

_Applicability:
This rule applies to websites, electronic documents, and any software that has a user interface.

This rule does not apply to content that is only used on hardware with a fixed display orientation or that has no sensor to detect or change the orientation.
_Requirement:
Content does not restrict its view and operation to a single display orientation, such as portrait or landscape, unless a specific display orientation is?[essential](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/orientation#dfn-essential). 

Note: Examples where a particular display orientation may be essential are a bank check, a piano application, slides for a projector or television, or virtual reality content where content is not necessarily restricted to landscape or portrait display orientation.
_Guidance: MAS 1.3.4 - Orientation is based on these standards: - WCAG: 1.3.4 Orientation - EN 301 549: PDF of EN 301 549, which applies WCAG principles for Orientation to 9.1.3.4 web, 10.1.3.4 non-web documents, and 11.1.3.4 software.

_Applicability:
This rule applies to websites, electronic documents, and any software that has a user interface.

This rule does not apply to non-web software and non-web documents that do not provide attributes that support identifying the expected meaning for the form input data.
_Requirement:
The purpose of each input field collecting information about the user can be programmatically determined when:
- The input field serves a purpose identified in the [Input Purposes for User Interface Components section](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/#input-purposes); and
- The content is implemented using technologies with support for identifying the expected meaning for form input data.
_Guidance: MAS 1.3.5 - Identify Input Purpose is based on these standards: - WCAG: 1.3.5 Identify Input Purpose - EN 301 549: PDF of EN 301 549, which applies WCAG principles for Identify Input Purpose to 9.1.3.5 web, 10.1.3.5 non-web documents, and 11.1.3.5.1 software.

_Requirement: Color is not used as the only visual means of conveying information, indicating an action, prompting a response, or distinguishing a visual element.
_DetectionPatterns: Information conveyed only through color differences
Links lacking underlines and relying on color alone to identify in blocks of text
Invalid form fields indicated only by red text (label, message or both) or border color
Required form fields vs optional form fields indicated by different label text colors
Chart data distinguished only by color
Status indicators using only color coding

PrimaryFixes.Principle: Provide additional non-color indicators alongside color coding
Use text, icons, or other visual cues in addition to color for status information
Examples: Error identifying text with red color

PrimaryFixes.Principle: Add patterns, labels, or other distinguishing features to color-coded data

ValidationCriteria: Information is available without color perception
All color-coded elements have non-color alternatives
Interface remains functional in grayscale
Where colors are used as unique identifiers, there is at least a 3:1 contrast ratio or greater between the colors

Good: Links within blocks of text are provided underlines as well as a color difference from static text
Error messages with both red color and error icon or explicit text that says 'error'
Required fields marked with asterisk (*) and red color
Charts using both color and patterns/symbols
Bad: Links lack an underline and do not have a 3:1 contrast difference compared to adjacent static text
Form errors shown only in red text and the text does not include the word 'error' or similar
Charts relying only on color coding
Status indicators using only color differences

_Applicability: This rule applies to websites, software, and electronic documents that support audio content.
_Requirement:
If any audio plays automatically for more than 3 seconds, either a ?[mechanism](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/#dfn-mechanism) ?is available to pause or stop the audio, or a mechanism is available to control audio volume independently from the overall system volume level. 

Video: [EN 301 549 Audio Control](https://www.youtube.com/watch?t=1079&v=-Youn7nq9GY&feature=youtu.be)
_Guidance: MAS 1.4.2 - Audio Control is based on these standards: - WCAG: 1.4.2 Audio Control - Section 508: E207.2 WCAG Conformance, E205.4 Accessibility Standard and E205.4.1 Word Substitution when Applying WCAG to Non-Web Documents, and E207.2.1 Word Substitution when Applying WCAG to Non-Web Software. - EN 301 549: PDF of EN 301 549, which applies WCAG principles for Audio Control to 9.1.4.2 web, 10.1.4.2 non-web documents, and 11.1.4.2 software.

_Requirement: Visible text must have a minimum luminosity contrast ratio of 4.5:1 against the background. Large-scale text (18 point or 14 point bold) must have a contrast ratio of at least 3:1. Exceptions include inactive UI components, pure decoration, invisible content, and logos.

exceptions.description: Text or images of text that are part of inactive user interface components
Pure decoration, not visible to anyone, or part of pictures with significant other visual content
Text that is part of a logo or brand name

_DetectionPatterns: Text with insufficient color contrast ratio
Normal text below 4.5:1 contrast ratio
Large text below 3:1 contrast ratio

PrimaryFixes.Principle: Adjust foreground or background colors to achieve minimum contrast ratios
Test with contrast analyzer tools and adjust until minimum ratios are met

ValidationCriteria: Normal text achieves 4.5:1 contrast ratio minimum
Large text achieves 3:1 contrast ratio minimum
Contrast maintained across different viewing conditions
Interactive element text contrast is below the minimum, but the interactive element is marked as disabled

Good: Black text on white background (21:1 ratio)
Dark blue (#003366) on white background (8.7:1 ratio)
White text on dark backgrounds with sufficient contrast
Low opacity text due to an interactive control being disabled
Bad: Light gray text on white backgrounds
Yellow text on white backgrounds
White text on orange backgrounds
Using only color differences without sufficient luminance contrast
Low opacity text due to an interactive control being disabled, but the control is still focusable or has some level of interactivity, e.g., it displays a tooltip on hover or focus

_Applicability:
This rule applies to websites, electronic documents, and any software that has a user interface.  

The rule does not apply to text that is [captions](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/#dfn-captions)?or?[images of text](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/#dfn-images-of-text).
_Requirement:
Ensure [text](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/#dfn-text)?can be resized without assistive technology up to 200% with no loss of content or functionality.  

Reference [Guideline 1.4.4 - Resize Text Resolution](https://microsoft.sharepoint.com/:w:/r/sites/accessibility/_layouts/15/Doc.aspx?sourcedoc=%7BB75CF91B-4D64-4408-9C2B-3359420D0D56%7D&file=Guideline%201.4.4%20%E2%80%93%20Resize%20Text%20Resolution.docx&action=default&mobileredirect=true&wdLOR=c38B87085-9A6E-4967-A1E9-79988BC4D143&cid=401c8dad-d537-4a5f-a4db-be0e25fd11f3&share=IQEb-Vy3ZE0IRJwrM1lCDQ1WAQihABcDGoOyLTGesAu9diE) for help meeting this accessibility standard.
_Guidance: MAS 1.4.4 -Resize Text is based on these standards: - WCAG: 1.4.4 Resize Text - Section 508: E207.2 WCAG Conformance, E205.4 Accessibility Standard and E205.4.1 Word Substitution when Applying WCAG to Non-Web Documents, and E207.2.1 Word Substitution when Applying WCAG to Non-Web Software. - EN 301 549: PDF of EN 301 549, which applies WCAG principles for Resize Text to 9.1.4.4 web, 10.1.4.4 non-web documents, and 11.1.4.4.1 software.

_Applicability:
This rule applies to websites, electronic documents, and any software that has a user interface.  

This rule does not apply if the image of text can be ?[visually customized](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/#dfn-visually-customized) ?to the user's requirements.
_Requirement: Ensure text is used instead of images of text when technology allows, unless it is [essential](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/#dfn-essential). Logotypes (text that is part of a logo or brand name) are considered essential and thus can remain images.
_Guidance: MAS 1.4.5 - Images of Text is based on these standards: - WCAG: 1.4.5 Images of Text - Section 508: E207.2 WCAG Conformance, E205.4 Accessibility Standard and E205.4.1 Word Substitution when Applying WCAG to Non-Web Documents, and E207.2.1 Word Substitution when Applying WCAG to Non-Web Software. - EN 301 549: PDF of EN 301 549, which applies WCAG principles for Images of Text to 9.1.4.5 web, 10.1.4.5 non-web documents, and 11.1.4.5.1 software.

_Applicability: This rule applies to websites, electronic documents, and any software that has a user interface.
_Requirement:
Content can be presented without loss of information or functionality, and without requiring scrolling in two dimensions for:

- Vertical scrolling content at a width equivalent to 320 [CSS pixels](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/reflow#dfn-css-pixel); - Horizontal scrolling content at a height equivalent to 256 [CSS pixels](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/reflow#dfn-css-pixel);

Except for parts of the content which require two-dimensional layout for usage or meaning.

Note: 320 CSS pixels is equivalent to a starting viewport width of 1280 CSS pixels wide at 400% zoom. For web content which is designed to scroll horizontally (e.g., with vertical text), 256 CSS pixels is equivalent to a starting viewport height of 1024 CSS pixels at 400% zoom.

Note: Examples of content which requires two-dimensional layout are images required for understanding (such as maps and diagrams), video, games, presentations, data tables (not individual cells), and interfaces where it is necessary to keep toolbars in view while manipulating content. It is acceptable to provide two-dimensional scrolling for such parts of the content.
_Guidance: MAS 1.4.10 - Reflow is based on these standards: - WCAG: 1.4.10 Reflow - EN 301 549: PDF of EN 301 549, which applies WCAG principles for Reflow to 9.1.4.10 web, 10.1.4.10 non-web documents, and 11.1.4.10 software.

_Applicability:
This rule applies to websites, electronic documents, and any software that has a user interface. This rule does not apply in the following situations: **User Interface Components:**
inactive components or where the appearance of the component is determined by the user agent or platform software and not modified by the author. **Graphical Objects:**
when a particular presentation of graphics is?[essential](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/#dfn-essential)?to the information being conveyed.
_Requirement:
The visual [presentation](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/#dfn-presentation) of the following have a [contrast ratio](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/#dfn-contrast-ratio) of at least 3:1 against adjacent color(s): - **User Interface Components:**
Visual information used to indicate [states](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/#dfn-states) and boundaries of [user interface components](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/#dfn-user-interface-components), except for inactive components or where the appearance of the component is determined by the user agent or platform software and not modified by the author. Any visual information necessary to indicate state, such as whether a component is selected or focused must also ensure that the information used to identify the control in that state has a minimum 3:1 contrast ratio. - This does not require that changes in color that differentiate between states of an individual component meet the 3:1 contrast ratio when they do not appear next to each other. For example, there is not a new requirement that visited links contrast with the default color, or that mouse hover indicators contrast with the default state. However, the component must not lose contrast with the adjacent colors, and non-text indicators such as the check in a checkbox or an arrow graphic indicating a menu is selected or open must have sufficient contrast to the adjacent colors. - This does not require that controls have a visual boundary indicating the hit area, but if the visual indicator of the control is the only way to identify the control, then that indicator must have sufficient contrast. If text (or an icon) within a button or placeholder text inside a text input is visible and there is no visual indication of the hit area then the requirement is met. If a button with text also has a colored border, since the border does not provide the only indication there is no contrast requirement beyond the text contrast (1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum)). Note that for people with cognitive disabilities it is recommended to delineate the boundary of controls to aid in the recognition of controls and therefore the completion of activities.

- **Graphical Objects:**
Parts of graphics required to understand the content, except when a particular presentation of graphics is [essential](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/#dfn-essential) to the information being conveyed.
_Guidance: MAS 1.4.11 - Non-text Contrast is based on these standards: - WCAG: 1.4.11 Non-text Contrast - EN 301 549: PDF of EN 301 549, which applies WCAG principles for Non-text Content to 9.1.4.11 web, 10.1.4.11 non-web documents, and 11.1.4.11 software.

_Applicability: This rule applies to websites, electronic documents, and any software that has a user interface.
_Guidance: MAS 1.4.12 - Text Spacing is based on these standards: - WCAG: 1.4.12 Text Spacing - EN 301 549: PDF of EN 301 549, which applies WCAG principles for Text Spacing to 9.1.4.12 web, 10.1.4.12 non-web documents, and 11.1.4.12 software.

_Requirement: Where receiving and then removing pointer hover or keyboard focus triggers additional content to become visible and then hidden, the content must be dismissible, hoverable, and persistent according to specific criteria.

exceptions.description: Visual presentation controlled by user agent or platform software and not modified by author

_DetectionPatterns: Tooltips or popups that cannot be dismissed without moving focus
Hover content that disappears when trying to interact with it
Focus-triggered content that doesn't persist appropriately
Additional content that obscures other interface elements

PrimaryFixes.Principle: Provide mechanism to dismiss additional content without moving hover or focus
Allow pointer to move over additional content without it disappearing
Examples: Maintain popup when hovering over its content
Provide connection between trigger and popup

PrimaryFixes.Principle: Keep additional content visible until trigger is removed or user dismisses it
Examples: Manual dismiss required for important content

ValidationCriteria: Additional content can be dismissed without removing trigger
Users can interact with hover-triggered content
Content persists until appropriately dismissed

Good: Tooltips dismissible with Escape key
Dropdown menus that stay open when hovering over content
Help popups that persist until manually closed
Bad: Tooltips that can only be dismissed by moving mouse away
Menus that close when trying to click on items
Content that disappears unexpectedly

_Requirement: All functionality of the content is operable through a keyboard interface without requiring specific timings for individual keystrokes, except where the underlying function requires input that depends on the path of the user's movement and not just the endpoints.

exceptions.description: Functions that require input depending on the path of user's movement (e.g., handwriting)

_DetectionPatterns: Interactive elements not reachable by keyboard
Mouse-only interactions without keyboard alternatives
Custom controls without keyboard support
Keyboard traps where focus cannot be moved away

PrimaryFixes.Principle: Ensure all interactive elements can be reached and activated using only keyboard
Provide keyboard equivalent for all mouse interactions
Implement standard keyboard navigation patterns for custom components

ValidationCriteria: All interactive content reachable via keyboard
All functionality available via keyboard
Keyboard focus moves logically through interface

Good: Standard HTML controls (buttons, links) with built-in keyboard support
Custom controls with ARIA roles and keyboard event handlers
Logical tab order through interactive elements
Bad: Click-only buttons without keyboard support
Custom dropdowns without arrow key navigation
Modal dialogs that trap keyboard focus

_Requirement: If keyboard focus can be moved to a component using a keyboard interface, then focus can be moved away from that component using only a keyboard interface, and, if it requires more than unmodified arrow or tab keys or other standard exit methods, the user is advised of the method for moving focus away.
_DetectionPatterns: Modal dialogs that trap focus without escape method
Custom widgets where Tab key doesn't move focus away
Embedded content that captures keyboard focus
Components requiring non-standard exit methods without instructions

PrimaryFixes.Principle: Ensure modal dialogs can be closed using standard keyboard methods
Examples: Focus returns to triggering element on close

PrimaryFixes.Principle: Allow users to exit custom widgets using standard or documented keyboard methods
Examples: Arrow keys for internal navigation only

PrimaryFixes.Principle: Provide clear instructions for non-standard keyboard navigation patterns

ValidationCriteria: Users can always exit components using keyboard
Standard exit methods work as expected
Non-standard exit methods are clearly documented

Good: Modal dialogs closable with Escape key
Tab navigation that cycles through and exits components
Clear instructions for complex keyboard interactions
Bad: Modals with no keyboard exit method
Widgets that capture Tab key permanently
Complex interactions without usage instructions

_Applicability: This rule applies to websites, electronic documents, and any software that has a user interface.
_Requirement:
If a [keyboard shortcut](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/#dfn-keyboard-shortcuts) is implemented in content using only letter (including upper- and lower-case letters), punctuation, number, or symbol characters, then at least one of the following is true: - **Turn off** A [mechanism](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/#dfn-mechanism) is available to turn off the shortcut.

- **Remap** A mechanism is available to remap the shortcut to use one or more non-printable keyboard characters (e.g. Ctrl, Alt, et cetera).

- **Active only on focus** The keyboard shortcut for a [user interface component](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/#dfn-user-interface-components) is only active when that component has focus.

NOTE: A long press of a key (2 seconds or more) and other accessibility features provided by the platform do not meet the [definition of a keyboard shortcut](https://www.w3.org/TR/wcag2ict-22/#dfn-keyboard-shortcut).
_Guidance: MAS 2.1.4 -Character Key Shortcuts is based on these standards: - WCAG: 2.1.4 Character Key Shortcuts - EN 301 549: PDF of EN 301 549, which applies WCAG principles for Character Key Shortcuts to 9.2.1.4 web, 10.2.1.4 non-web documents, and 11.2.1.4.1 software.

_Applicability: This rule applies to websites, electronic documents, and any software that has a user interface.
_Requirement:
For any feature that requires users to complete an action within a set period of time, at least one of the following is true: 

**Turn off**: The user is allowed to turn off the time limit before encountering it; **OR** 

**Adjust**: The user is allowed to adjust the time limit before encountering it over a wide range that is at least ten times the length of the default setting; **OR** 

**Extend**: The user is warned before time expires and given at least 20 seconds to extend the time limit with a simple action (for example, "press the space bar"), and the user is allowed to extend the time limit at least ten times; **OR** 

**Real-time** 
The time limit is a required part of a real-time event (for example, gameplay or a live auction), and no alternative to the time limit is possible; **OR**

**Essential** 
The time limit is essential and extending it would invalidate the activity; **OR**

**20 Hour** 
The time limit is longer than 20 hours.

_Applicability:
This rule applies to websites, electronic documents, and any software that has a user interface and interprets pointer actions. 

This rule does not apply to actions that are required to operate the user agent, underlying platform software, or assistive technology.
_Requirement:
For [functionality](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/#dfn-functionality) that can be operated using a [single pointer](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/#dfn-single-pointer), at least one of the following is true: - **No Down-Event:**
The [down-event](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/#dfn-down-event) of the pointer is not used to execute any part of the function;

- **Abort or Undo:**
Completion of the function is on the [up-event](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/#dfn-up-event), and a [mechanism](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/#dfn-mechanism) is available to abort the function before completion or to undo the function after completion;

- **Up Reversal:**
The up-event reverses any outcome of the preceding down-event;

- **Essential:**
Completing the function on the down-event is [essential](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/#dfn-essential).

Note: Functions that emulate a keyboard or numeric keypad key press are considered essential. Examples of essential functionality for non-web software are features for meeting environmental energy usage requirements (like waking a device from sleep, power saver mode, and low power state).

**As of September 21, 2023, this requirement has been deprecated. It no longer needs to be tested and should always be marked �Supports�.**

In content implemented using markup languages, elements have complete start and end tags, elements are nested according to their specifications, elements do not contain duplicate attributes, and any IDs are unique, except where the specifications allow these features.

Note: This Success Criterion should be considered as always satisfied for any content using HTML or XML.

Although the HTML Standard treats some of these cases as non-conforming for authors, it is considered to "allow these features" for the purposes of this Success Criterion because the specification requires that user agents support handling these cases consistently. In practice, this criterion no longer provides any benefit to people with disabilities in itself.

_Requirement: For all user interface components, the name and role can be programmatically determined; states, properties, and values that can be set by the user can be programmatically set; and notification of changes to these items is available to user agents, including assistive technologies.
_DetectionPatterns: Interactive elements without accessible names
Custom components missing ARIA roles
Form controls without proper labels
Invalid nesting of interactive elements within other interactive elements
Misuse of aria-hidden on elements that contain focusable elements, or are already hidden with CSS display: none or visibility: hidden
Dynamic content changes not announced to assistive technology

PrimaryFixes.Principle: Provide accessible names for all interactive elements using labels, the element's text content, or ARIA attributes. ARIA attributes should only be used as a last resort when other methods are not feasible.
Examples: provide visible text within a button or link to name it
alt text for images within buttons and links
aria-labelledby for elements with visible text labels that can't use the label element
use aria-label to name elements that don't have visible text labels or already use other naming techniques

PrimaryFixes.Principle: Accessible names should not be provided to generic elements (e.g., divs or spans) or elements with roles that ARIA prohibits from having an accessible name.
Examples: remove aria-label from generic div elements, or provide the div with an appropriate ARIA role that allows it to have an accessible name

do not use aria-label or aria-labelledby on label elements. Instead, if a form control needs an accessible name that has more information than what is present in the visible label, then use aria-describedby to provide additional information about the form control

if an element has role=none or role=presentation, remove any aria-label or aria-labelledby attributes from the element. An element can't be marked as presentational and also provided an accessible name
do not use aria-label to repeat the visible text of a control, exactly

PrimaryFixes.Principle: Use the appropriate native HTML element, or define appropriate ARIA roles for custom components to communicate their purpose. Prioritize using native HTML over ARIA whenever possible.
Examples: use the button element, or role='button' for custom buttons
use the nav element or role='navigation' for nav areas
use the dialog element or role='dialog' for modal dialogs

PrimaryFixes.Principle: Communicate component states and properties using the appropriate HTML or ARIA attributes. Do not use both native HTML attributes and ARIA attribute counterparts for the same state or property, as this could result in conflicts. Prioritize using native HTML attributes over ARIA whenever possible.
Examples: the checked attribute for native checkboxes or aria-checked for custom ARIA checkboxes
the disabled attribute or aria-disabled for inactive elements

PrimaryFixes.Principle: Use aria-hidden=true to hide content from assistive technologies only when the content is still visually present. If content is hidden from all users, use CSS display: none or visibility: hidden instead. If using aria-hidden=true to hide content from assistive technologies, ensure that the content does not contain focusable elements, as this can result in inaccessible content.
Examples: if content is hidden from all users, use display: none or visibility: hidden instead of aria-hidden=true

if using aria-hidden=true to hide content from assistive technologies, if there are focusable elements within the aria-hidden=true container, either ensure they are set to disabled or have been removed from the document focus order (e.g., with tabindex=-1)
if content is meant to be inert, use the inert attribute instead of using aria-hidden=true and attempting to ensure focusable content cannot be focused
do not use inert for elements that should be marked as disabled

PrimaryFixes.Principle: Elements with interactive roles (widts) should not be nested within other interactive elements, as this can result in the name, role and value/state of the nested element or its parent being incorrectly exposed, or completely inaccessible.
Examples: a button cannot be specified within a button, option, menuitem, etc.
links cannot contain other interactive elements
if a design calls for what appears to be interactive elements, make sure the elements are instead siblings, and use CSS to position the elements to appear as if they are nested, when necessary

ValidationCriteria: Interactive elements must never be nested within other elements with interactive roles
All interactive elements have accessible names
Component roles are properly defined or the native HTML equivalent is used
States and properties are programmatically available
Focusable elements cannot be accessed if they are within an aria-hidden=true container element

Good: Form inputs with associated label elements
Buttons with descriptive text or aria-label if visible text is not present
Custom components with the required ARIA roles and properties
Use display: none or visibility: hidden instead of aria-hidden=true to hide content from assistive technologies when the content is also visually hidden
Bad: Buttons visually presented with only an icon and no text or aria-label
aria-labels that repeat the same text as visible content
title attributes that repeat the same text as the aria-label or visible text content
interactive elements that have nested interactive elements within them
Form inputs without associated labels
Using aria-hidden=true when an element is already set to display: none or visibility: hidden
Interactive elements or components without ARIA roles

_Applicability:
This rule applies to authoring tools. An authoring tool is *any software that can be used by authors, alone or collaboratively, to create or modify content or to develop applications or services, for use by other people (other authors or end users)*.

Notes: � �Content� includes documents, websites, blogs, images, video, and user-generated content. � Any software that offers an ability for authors or end users to create rich text content is considered an authoring tool. � Any software that **only** offers an ability for authors or end users to create plain text content is **not** considered an authoring tool.

This rule does not apply when the authoring tool is used to directly edit plain text or plain text source code.
_Requirement:
Authoring tools must enable users to create or edit applications, services, tools, and content that is accessible. Authoring tools shall permit authors the option of overriding information required for accessibility.

Notes: � Authoring tools may rely on additional tools to create accessible content **only if** it is not achievable (i.e., technically possible) in a single tool. � For video creation and editing tools, this requirement includes supporting the creation and editing of videos with closed captions and audio descriptions. � This requirement includes enabling users to edit video captions and transcripts created using automatic speech recognition for accuracy.

Note: If option (2) is utilized, customer conformance statements relating to this requirement should explain in the "remarks and explanation" field that we use technology that meets or exceeds the audio quality provided by and G.722.2 / IETF RFC 6716.

_Applicability: This rule applies if your product or service supports two-way voice communication.�
_Requirement:
Information and communication technology (ICT) products and services that support two-way voice communication must also support Real-Time Text (RTT).

RTT?means text communications that are transmitted over?IP networks immediately as they are created (i.e.,?on a character-by-character basis).?The text is sent immediately without the user needing to hit �send�. RTT is?the successor technology to?Text Telephone?([MAS 6.5 - TTY](https://aka.ms/MAS6.5)) as TTY does not operate reliably?on IP networks.? 

**United States:** Under U.S. law, mobile handsets and other devices for use with IP-based voice services from wireless carriers must support RTT. Because wireless carriers define the technical implementations of RTT,?individual carrier device specifications should be consulted to determine detailed engineering requirements. 

**Canada:** As of December 31, 2020, under Canadian law, wireless service providers must implement RTT for communication with emergency services.?Because wireless service providers define the technical implementations of RTT, individual service provider device specifications should be consulted to determine detailed engineering requirements. 

**European Union:** As of June 28, 2025, under EU law, products and services supporting two-way voice communication must support RTT for point to point and multi-party calls. The technical specifications of EN 301 549 listed in the Standards section below should be followed to meet this requirement but note that the definition of RTT in EU law differs from EN 301 549 in that the law explicitly requires the text to be sent on a character-by-character basis. ETSI Technical Report (TR) 103 708 �Real-Time Text in Multiparty Conference Calling� provides guidance for multi-party RTT support and proposes corresponding changes to EN 301 549, though it has not yet been officially adopted (as of February 2024).

_Title: Requirements for Voice Mail, Auto Attendants, and IVR
_Applicability: This rule applies to products and services that provide two-way voice communication and voicemail, auto-attendant, or interactive voice response (IVR).
_Requirement:
Where information and communication technology (ICT) provides real-time voice-based communication and also provides voice mail, auto-attendant, or interactive voice response (IVR) facilities, the ICT shall offer users a means to access the information and carry out the tasks provided by the ICT without the use of hearing or speech. Where provided, voice mail, auto-attendant, interactive voice response, and caller identification systems shall be usable with a TTY. 

Note: Tasks that involve both operating the interface and perceiving the information would require that both the interface and information be accessible without use of speech or hearing. 

Additionally, voicemail, IVR systems, and related telecommunication functions that provide playback must include player controls that allow users to pause, skip, rewind, and repeat all messages and prompts.
_Guidance: MAS 6.4 - Requirements for Voice Mail, Auto Attendants, and IVR is based on these standards: - Section 508: 412.8.4 Voice Mail and Other Messaging Systems - EN 301 549: 6.4 Alternatives to voice-based services (PDF) - Section 255: 47 CFR 7.5

_Applicability: Any device that includes a voice cellular antenna must meet requirements related to Text Telephone (TTY). Voice over IP (VoIP) services that are interconnected with the PSTN must support TTY.

Information and communication technology (ICT) equipment or systems with two-way voice communication that do not themselves provide TTY functionality shall provide the following: - TTY connectability � ICT shall provide a standard non-acoustic connection point for TTYs. - Voice and Hearing Carry Over � ICT shall provide a microphone capable of being easily turned on and off to allow the user to intermix speech with TTY use. - Signal Compatibility � ICT shall support all commonly used cross-manufacturer non-proprietary standard TTY signal protocols where the system interoperates with the Public Switched Telephone Network (PSTN).

In the US, the FCC considers real-time text (RTT) support to be an acceptable substitute for TTY support. Voice communication services subject to this requirement that are provided over wireless IP facilities and equipment used with such services are not required to provide TTY support if such services and equipment support RTT. See [MAS 6.2 � Real-Time Text (RTT) Functionality](https://aka.ms/mas6.2) for further information.

_Title: User Interfaces, Video Programming Guides and Menus
_Applicability:
This rule applies to: - Devices that receive or playback video programming (such as the Xbox One, Xbox 360, Xbox Blu-ray/DVD player, PCs, Phones and Tablets, Surface, and Surface Hub), - Devices that have preinstalled video applications, whether our own or third party (such as the Xbox OneGuide, Microsoft Movies & TV, Groove, Windows Media Player, and preinstalled third-party applications such as Netflix, Hulu, or Amazon), and - Video applications that we direct people to use to access video programming,

If those devices have - Onscreen menus that offer any of 11 specific video playback functions, or - Offer video playback functionality in a manner other than onscreen text menus, such as a power on/off on hardware.
_Requirement:
Any User Interface (UI) that a person must navigate in order to launch applications that play video programming must be accompanied by audio output (such as through a screen reader). The following functions, if offered through an onscreen text menu, must be accompanied by audible output: 1. Power on / off 2. Volume adjust / mute 3. Channel / program selection (including on-demand programming) 4. Display channel / program information (including on-demand programming) 5. Configuration / set-up (for example, language selection, parental controls) 6. Enable / disable closed captioning 7. Configuration of closed captioning options (for example, changing font size, color) 8. Enable / disable video description 9. Display configuration info 10. Playback functions (for example, play, pause, rewind, fast forward, stop, and record) 11. Input selection.

Covered devices and applications are not required to include any or all of these functions, but if they are included, they must be accessible.

If any of these 11 functions are offered other than through on-screen menus (for example, power-on functionality could be activated via the hardware) then those functions must still be accessible for individuals without vision, with low vision and limited or no hearing, and with limited or no color perception.

A feature is "accessible" if the input, control, and mechanical functions are locatable, identifiable, and operable for a person with a disability. A person with a disability should have at least one method for using the feature that provides equivalent functionality as is available to users without a disability. For example, the power-on mechanical control should be tactilely discernable to aid use by individuals with visual impairments; patterns should be used to augment color cues for those with limited color perception.

Video programming is programming by, or comparable to, programming provided by a television broadcast station, including when such video programming is delivered using Internet Protocol (IP). It does not include user-generated content, unless that content is subsequently broadcast on television with captions.
_Guidance: MAS 7.6 � User Interfaces, Video Programming Guides and Menus is based on these regulations: - FCC: 47 CFR �79.107(a) User interfaces provided by digital apparatus

_Title: Secondary Audio Stream Support for Recording Devices and Video Players that Support Linear Programming
_Applicability:
This rule applies to:

- Devices that receive, play back, or record video programming (such as but not limited to the Xbox One, Xbox 360, Xbox Blu-ray/DVD player, PCs, Phones and Tablets, and Surface);
- Devices that have preinstalled video applications, our own or third party (such as the Xbox OneGuide, Microsoft Movies & TV, Groove, Windows Media Player, or preinstalled third-party applications such as Netflix, Hulu, or Amazon); and
- Players that are preinstalled or that Microsoft directs consumers to use in order to access linear programming on our devices (such as Xbox TV).
_Requirement:
Video players that support linear programming (that is, prescheduled television programming via cable, satellite or over the air) and players that record video programming comparable to that provided by broadcasters must support the secondary audio stream to enable the transmission of audio emergency information.

Linear programming is prescheduled (as opposed to on-demand) broadcast programming delivered via cable, satellite, or over the air.

_Title: Hearing Aid Compatibility (HAC) for Mobile Handsets (T mode)
_Applicability: This rule applies if the mobile handset is used with voice communication services over a mobile operator's cellular network. A phablet is considered a mobile handset for this purpose. A tablet or PC that is not typically held to the ear is not considered a mobile handset covered by this rule.
_Requirement:
Mobile handsets must provide a means of magnetic coupling with hearing technologies (e.g., hearing aids, cochlear implants and assistive listening devices). Note that in 2021, the FCC adopted a new standard to use in certifying mobile devices as compliant with Hearing Aid Compatibility (HAC) requirements, as described below. Compliance with that standard, ANSI C63.19-2019, will be required for all devices submitted to the FCC for certification on or after December 5, 2023.

**Before December 5, 2023**, handsets submitted to the FCC for equipment certification must have a rating of T3 or T4 associated with the ANSI C63.19-2011 standard or meet the ANSI C63.19-2019 standard to be compliant with HAC. "T" refers to the phone's coupling ability and is intended for use with hearing aids in the telecoil mode.

**On or after December 5, 2023**, handsets submitted to the FCC for equipment certification must meet the ANSI C63.19-2019 standard to be compliant with HAC. The FCC has waived some of the volume control test procedures in ANSI C63.19-2019 until September 29, 2025. See the FCC�s [hearing aid compatibility guidance documents](https://apps.fcc.gov/oetcf/kdb/forms/FTSSearchResultPage.cfm?switch=P&id=36388) (KDB publication 285076) for further information on testing handsets..

Note that the ANSI C63.19-2019 standard replaces the numerical M/T rating system with a different set of requirements and thresholds to determine hearing aid compatibility. In addition to testing the phone�s coupling ability, the ANSI C63.19-2019 standard requires that handsets meet the volume control specifications of the ANSI/TIA-5050:2018 standard to be considered HAC-compliant.
_Guidance:
MAS 8.6 - Hearing Aid Compatibility (HAC) for Mobile Handsets (T mode) is based on these standards: - Section 508: 412.3.1 Wireless Handsets

ICT in the form of wireless handsets shall conform to ANSI/IEEE C63.19-2011 (incorporated by reference, see [702.5.1](https://www.access-board.gov/ict/#702.5.1)).

- EN 301 549: 8.2.2.2 Wireless communication devices (PDF)

Where ICT hardware is a wireless communication device with speech output which is normally held to the ear, it shall provide a means of magnetic coupling to hearing technologies which meets the requirements of ETSI ES 200 381-2 [3].

NOTE: ICT fulfilling the requirements of ANSI/IEEE C63.19 [2011] is deemed to comply with the requirements of this clause.

- FCC: 47 CFR �20.19(b) Hearing aid compatibility; technical standards

(b) Hearing aid compatibility; technical standards�(1) Handset compatibility on or after June 5, 2023. In order to satisfy a manufacturer or service provider's obligations under paragraphs (c) and (d) of this section, a handset submitted for equipment certification or for a permissive change relating to hearing aid compatibility on or after June 5, 2023 must meet the 2019 ANSI standard [ANSI C63.19-2019].

(2) Handset compatibility before June 5, 2023. In order to satisfy a manufacturer or service provider's obligations under paragraphs (c) and (d) of this section, a handset submitted for equipment certification or for a permissive change relating to hearing aid compatibility before June 5, 2023 must meet either:

(i) At a minimum, the M3 and T3 ratings associated with the 2011 ANSI standard; or

(ii) The 2019 ANSI standard.

(3) Handsets operating over multiple frequency bands or air interfaces.

(i) Beginning on June 5, 2023, a handset is hearing aid-compatible if it meets the 2019 ANSI standard for all frequency bands that are specified in the ANSI standard and all air interfaces over which it operates on those frequency bands, and the handset has been certified as compliant with the test requirements for the 2019 ANSI standard pursuant to �2.1033(d) of this chapter.

(ii) Before June 5, 2023, a handset that uses only the frequencies specified in the 2011 ANSI standard is hearing aid-compatible with regard to radio frequency interference and inductive coupling if it meets the 2011 ANSI standard for all frequency bands and air interfaces over which it operates, and the handset has been certified as compliant with the test requirements for the 2011 ANSI standard pursuant to �2.1033(d) of this chapter. Before June 5, 2023, a handset that incorporates operations outside the frequencies specified in the 2011 ANSI standard is hearing aid-compatible if the handset otherwise satisfies the requirements of this paragraph (b).

(4) Factual questions. All factual questions of whether a handset meets the technical standard(s) of this paragraph (b) shall be referred for resolution to the Chief, Office of Engineering and Technology, Federal Communications Commission, 45 L Street NE, Washington, DC 20554.

_Title: Hearing Aid Compatibility (HAC) for Mobile Handsets (M mode)
_Applicability: This rule applies if the mobile handset is manufactured or imported for use in the United States (including US territories) and is used with voice communications. A phablet is considered a mobile handset for this purpose. A tablet or PC that is not typically held to the ear is not considered a mobile handset covered by this rule.
_Requirement:
Mobile handsets must reduce interference with hearing technologies (e.g., hearing aids, cochlear implants and assistive listening devices) to the lowest possible level that will allow use of the product. Note that in 2021, the FCC adopted a new standard to use in certifying mobile devices as compliant with Hearing Aid Compatibility (HAC) requirements, as described below. Compliance with that standard, ANSI C63.19-2019, will be required for all devices submitted to the FCC for certification on or after December 5, 2023.

**Before December 5, 2023**, handsets submitted to the FCC for equipment certification must have a rating of M3 or M4 associated with the ANSI C63.19-2011 standard or meet the ANSI C63.19-2019 standard to be compliant with HAC. "M" refers to the microphone mode.

**On or after December 5, 2023**, handsets submitted to the FCC for equipment certification must meet the ANSI C63.19-2019 standard to be compliant with HAC. The FCC has waived some of the volume control test procedures in ANSI C63.19-2019 until September 29, 2025. See the FCC�s [hearing aid compatibility guidance documents](https://apps.fcc.gov/oetcf/kdb/forms/FTSSearchResultPage.cfm?switch=P&id=36388) (KDB publication 285076) for further information on testing handsets.

Note that the ANSI C63.19-2019 standard replaces the numerical M/T rating system with a different set of requirements and thresholds to determine hearing aid compatibility. In addition to testing the phone in microphone mode, the ANSI C63.19-2019 standard requires that handsets meet the volume control specifications of the ANSI/TIA-5050:2018 standard to be considered HAC-compliant.
_Guidance:

_Applicability: This rule applies to platforms (e.g., operating systems).
_Requirement:
Where software is a platform (e.g., an operating system), it must provide the following assistive technology experiences and provide discoverable UI to configure and change them:
�	Enable sequential entry of multiple (chorded) keystrokes; (e.g. Sticky Keys)
�	Provide adjustment of delay before key acceptance (e.g. Filter Keys)
�	Provide adjustment of delay before key acceptance with a delay range that includes 0.5 seconds (e.g. Slow Keys)
�	Provide adjustment of same-key double-strike acceptance with delay adjustable over a range that includes 2 seconds (e.g. Repeat Keys)
�	Allow users to choose visual alternative for audio output (e.g. Notifications in Action Center)
�	Synchronize audio equivalents for visual events (e.g. Notification Sounds and Sound Sentry) 
�	Provide speech output services (e.g. Windows Narrator)
�	Display any captions provided (e.g. Closed Captions)

_Applicability: This rule applies when a biometric form of identification, such as fingerprints or iris patterns, is required (for example, in websites, software, services, or hardware).
_Requirement: Products or services that use a biometric form of user identification must provide an alternative method for identification that is either non-biometric (e.g., entering a password) or a second biometric form using dissimilar biological characteristics (e.g., using a retinal scan instead of a fingerprint).
_Guidance: MAS 11.2 - Biometric ID is based on these standards: - Section 508: 403.1 General - EN 301 549: 5.3 Biometrics (PDF)

_Applicability: This rule applies to software and operating systems.
_Requirement:
Where ICT with key repeat is provided and the key repeat cannot be turned off:
a) the delay before the key repeat shall be adjustable to at least 2 seconds; and
b) the key repeat rate shall be adjustable down to one character per 2 seconds.
_Guidance: MAS 11.3.1 - Key Repeat is based on these standards: - EN 301 549: 5.7 Key repeat (PDF)

_Applicability: This rule applies to software and operating systems.
_Requirement: Where a keyboard or keypad is provided, the delay after any keystroke, during which an additional key-press will not be accepted if it is identical to the previous keystroke, shall be adjustable up to at least 0,5 seconds.
_Guidance: MAS 11.3.2 - Double Strike Key Acceptance is based on these standards: - EN 301 549: 5.8 Double-strike key acceptance (PDF)

_Applicability: This rule applies to software and hardware.
_Requirement:
Have at least one mode of operation and information retrieval that does not require simultaneous user actions. No feature should require more than one control to be activated simultaneously to operate it. However, sequential operation of two controls to engage a feature is acceptable via menu or special operating mode the user can select and de-select.

Having to use both hands to open the lid of a laptop, having to press two or more keys at the same time or having to touch a surface with more than one finger are examples of simultaneous user actions.
_Guidance: MAS 11.3.3 - Simultaneous User Actions is based on these standards: - EN 301 549: 5.9 Simultaneous user actions (PDF)

_Applicability: This rule applies to products, services, and tools that transmit, receive, or process data, file formats, or content.
_Requirement: Information and communication technology (ICT) shall preserve all accessibility information for any format or standard that it supports when transmitting, receiving, converting or processing data, file formats, or content.
_Guidance: MAS 11.4 - Preserving Accessibility Information is based on these standards: - Section 508: 404.1 Preservation of Information Provided for Accessibility - EN 301 549: 5.4 Preservation of accessibility information during conversion (PDF)

_Applicability: This rule applies to products and services that use interconnected or non-interconnected VoIP for in-game chat.
_Requirement:
For Voice over IP (VoIP, both interconnected and non-interconnected) services used during in-game chat, implementation of the Xbox and Windows platform speech-to-text/text-to-speech feature is required to make the audio chat accessible to people who cannot hear, have hearing loss, cannot speak, or have speech impairments.

A feature is �accessible� if the input, control, and mechanical functions are locatable, identifiable, and operable for a person with a disability.
_Guidance: MAS 11.5 - Speech-to-Text and Text-to-Speech for In-game Chat is based on these standards: - FCC: 47 CFR �14.20 � Obligations for Covered Communications Services - FCC: 47 CFR �14.21 � Performance Objectives

_Applicability: This rule applies to?ICT that has a locking or toggle control and that control is visually presented to the user.
_Requirement: Where information and communication technology (ICT) has a locking or toggle control and that control is visually presented to the user, there is at least one mode of operation where the status of all locking or toggle controls can be determined through touch or sound without operating the control.
_Guidance: MAS 11.7 - Tactile or Auditory Status is based on these standards: - EN 301 549: 5.6.1 Tactile or auditory status (PDF)

_Applicability: This rule applies to?ICT that has a locking or toggle control and that control is non-visually presented to the user.
_Requirement: Where information and communication technology (ICT) has a locking or toggle control and that control is non-visually presented to the user (such as through sound or touch), there is at least one mode of operation where the status of all locking or toggle controls can be visually determined when the control is presented.
_Guidance: MAS 11.8 - Visual Status is based on these standards: - EN 301 549: 5.6.2 Visual status (PDF)

_Applicability: This rule applies if your product is a self-contained, closed product that is a device unto itself. Examples include copiers, printers, fax machines, calculators, and information kiosks.
_Requirement:
Where information and communication technology (ICT) is closed or has closed functionality, that closed functionality shall be operable without requiring the user to attach, connect, or install assistive technology (not including personal headsets or induction loops).
Closed Functionality standards require that alternative access features be built into a product so users do not have to attach an assistive device to it. Additional requirements address mechanisms for private listening (handset or a standard headphone jack), touchscreens, auditory output and adjustable volume controls, and location of controls in accessible reach ranges.

_Applicability:
This rule applies if your product allows the running of applications by
providing an underlying software or hardware layer that serves as the
operating environment, architecture, or accessibility API(s).
_Requirement:
Platforms must provide UI that enable users to discover and change the
following accessibility settings:

-   High contrast

-   Foreground and background color as applied to the text and
    background of content

-   An alternative to audio alerts such as a visual alert (e.g., Windows
    Sound Sentry) or a tactile alert (e.g., vibrating phone)

-   System-level volume for platforms that enable audio presentation

-   Customized key input

    -   Modifier key lock such as Windows Sticky Keys

    -   Key input filter such as Windows Filter Keys

    -   Audio key lock such as Windows Toggle Keys

-   Customized text size up to 200%

-   Customized font type (must include one serif and one sans serif
    type)

-   Customized visual indication of user input focus

    -   Focus rectangle thickness

    -   Caret blink rate

    -   Caret width

    -   Mouse pointer size and color

-   Visual indication of keyboard shortcuts such as underline access
    keys

-   Alternative to mouse movement such as Windows Mouse Keys.

_Applicability:
Focus is used to indicate the specific UI element is ready to receive
input via a device or speech. As the user navigates and interacts with
the UI, focus changes from one element to another. UI elements that can
receive focus and are covered under this rule are interactive elements,
meaning they respond to user input. Examples include text, menus,
buttons, links, and list boxes.

For the purposes of MAS 06 - On Focus, input devices are defined as, but
not limited to:

-   Physical keyboards

-   On-screen keyboards

-   Xbox controllers

-   Media Center controllers (remote controls)

-   Keypads or buttons on handheld devices (both on-screen and hardware)

This applies to all configurations if a configuration is allowed that
includes attaching a keyboard or keypad with physical buttons. The
application and platform must be responsive to programmatic synthesis of
keyboard input even when a keyboard is not attached. This is critical to
techniques used by some assistive technology applications such as screen
readers and voice recognition software.

If your product or service does not support focus, or is in a mode where
focus behavior is not being used, then this rule does not apply. The
primary example is a touchscreen. All UI elements on a touchscreen
responding to touch or gestures are ready for input. No one element
currently "has focus."
_Requirement:
Avoid forced focus changes that are not initiated by the user. Ensure
all focus changes that occur are a result of user action and that the
user expects the change.

elements that can receive focus and are covered under this rule are
interactive elements, meaning they respond to user input. Examples

_Applicability:
This rule applies if your product has either of the following:

-   Includes or enables voice communications or other audio information
    over the public-switched telephone network (PSTN) or via Voice over
    IP (VOIP); and

-   Includes related functionality such as VoIP, voice mail, interactive
    voice response systems, caller ID, call waiting, call forwarding,
    speed dialing, repeat dialing, or computer provide directory
    assistance.
_Requirement:
Where ICT provides real-time voice-based communication and also provides
voice mail, auto-attendant, or interactive voice response facilities,
the ICT should offer users a means to access the information and carry
out the tasks provided by the ICT without the use of hearing or speech.

Additionally, voicemail, interactive voice response (IVR) systems, and
related telecommunication functions that provide playback must include
player controls that allow users to pause, skip, rewind, and repeat all
messages and prompts.

_Applicability:
This rule applies if your product has any of the following:

-   Enables voice communications, including VOIP

-   Enables video communications.

-   Enables real time (or near real time) human-to-human communication
    by text (such as email or SMS) and also provides audio output.
_Requirement:
Products that provide telecommunications or advanced communications
services (including interconnected and non-interconnected VoIP, Email,
instant messaging and video conferencing) must provide a way to allow
users to control volume. Where volume control is incremental, it shall
provide at least one intermediate step of 12 dB gain above the lowest
volume setting.

_Applicability:
This rule applies if your telecommunications product:

> has a handset, headset, earphone, or other transducer near the ear.
> Assume that the default volume level is safe, clear, and audible for
> fully able users. Note that personal communications devices such as
> cell phones do not typically default.
_Requirement:

an automatic volume reset function that sets the volume back to the
default level.

_Applicability:
This rule applies if your product has either of the following:

-   Allows the running of applications, by providing an underlying
    software or hardware layer, which serves as the operating
    environment, architecture or accessibility API(s). This includes,
    for example, Windows, Xbox, Windows Phone, but not Office, Microsoft
    Edge, or Azure.

interoperability with assistive technologies (ATs). For example, Windows
provides UI Automation (UIA).

that is a device unto itself. Examples include copiers, printers, fax
machines, calculators, and information kiosks.

be built into a product so users do not have to attach an assistive
device to it. Other specifications address mechanisms for private
listening (handset or a standard headphone jack), touchscreens, auditory
output and adjustable volume controls, and location of controls in
accessible reach ranges.

Does your product, service, tool or content run on a platform that
supports keyboard interfaces (such as physical or on-screen keyboard)
and allows user input or interaction?

-   If yes, this rule applies.

-   If no, this rule does not apply.
_Requirement:

text input, interaction with controls, and navigation) must be operable
through the UI by using only physical or on-screen keyboard interfaces
(on platforms that support keyboard interfaces). This includes a
requirement to support both onscreen and physical keyboards for mobile
apps.

Disabled controls may be in the tab order and they need to clearly
indicate that they are disabled.

_Applicability:
This rule applies if your product has any of the following:

-   User interface (anything the user sees, hears, or interacts with).
_Requirement:
Where software/application provides a user interface it shall interoperate with those documented [accessibility features](#accessibility-features-found-in-the-ease-of-access-settings-for-windows-10) that are defined in platform documentation. This includes ensuring that the following can be programmatically determined by the Platform assistive technology (usually via the use of Platform APIs): - role, state(s), boundary, name, and description; - row and column of each cell in a data table, including headers of the row and column if present; - the current value of a user interface element and any minimum or maximum values of the range; - relationship that a user interface element has as a label for another element, or of being labelled by another element; - relationship between a user interface element and any parent or children elements; - text contents, text attributes, and the boundary of text; - available actions that can be executed on a user interface element (and allow the programmatic execution of the actions); - information and mechanisms necessary to track focus, text insertion point, and selection attributes of user interface elements; - changes in those programmatically determinable attributes of user interface elements; Allow platform assistive technology to: - execute available actions on a user interface element; - modify track focus, text insertion point, and selection attributes of user interface elements; - programmatically modify states and properties of user interface elements; - modify values and text of user interface elements using the input methods of the platform; This also includes ensuring that [images and icons do not disappear when high contrast mode is enabled](http://blogs.msdn.com/b/wsdevsol/archive/2014/02/20/accessibility-gotchas-2-high-contrast.aspx). "Accessibility features" are defined as those found in the new "modern" Ease of Access Settings (Settings \> Ease of Access), not the old Ease of Access Center. _Applicability:

use in the United States (including US territories) and is used with
voice communication services over a mobile operator"s cellular network.

PC that is not typically held to the ear is not considered a mobile
handset covered by this rule.

technologies (e.g., hearing aids, cochlear implants and assistive
listening devices) with an FCC rating of T3 or T4. "T" refers to the
phone"s coupling ability and is intended for use with hearing aids in
the telecoil mode. The "T" rating of HAC-compliant devices must be
included on product packages or in product literature.

_Title: Hearing Aid Compatibility (HAC) for Mobile Handsets (M mode)
_Applicability:
This rule applies if the mobile handset is manufactured or imported for
use in the United States (including US territories) and is used with
voice communication services over a mobile operator"s cellular network.
A phablet is considered a mobile handset for this purpose. A tablet or
PC that is not typically held to the ear is not considered a mobile
handset covered by this rule.
_Requirement:
Mobile handsets must reduce interference with hearing technologies
(e.g., hearing aids, cochlear implants and assistive listening devices)
to the lowest possible level that will allow use of the product. To be
compliant with Hearing Aid Compatibility (HAC), the phone must have an
FCC rating of M3 or M4. "M" refers to the microphone mode. The "M"
rating of HAC-compliant devices must be included on product packages or
in product literature.
